claim_value: Urban forestry: Premier street/park tree. Nut orchards: Commercial ginkgo nut production in Asia. Medicinal plantations: Leaf extract (EGb 761) production. Windbreaks. Carbon sequestration. Shade tree.

Natural habitat: Occurs in deciduous forests in China; specific associates poorly documented due to rarity. Temple groves: Often planted with Cryptomeria, Podocarpus. No significant ecological community associations in modern era due to relict status.
Young: Smooth, grayish. Mature: Gray-brown, deeply furrowed and ridged; corky texture. Inner wood: Yellowish. Fire-resistant. Old trees may develop chichi aerial roots from branches.

Temperature: Survives -3.3 to 23.3C mean annual; tolerates USDA Zone 3 (-40C). Drought: Tolerant once established. Rainfall: 34-3925mm (extremely wide range). Climate zones: Entire temperate and Mediterranean range.

Highly adaptable. Optimum: Deep, well-draining, fertile soils. pH: 5.0-5.5 optimal; tolerates alkaline. Tolerates: Heavy clay, loam, sandy, compacted urban soils. Best: Sandy loam with good drainage. Sensitive to: Persistent waterlogging.

IUCN Red List: Endangered (EN). EDGE priority: High conservation priority. China status: Level I protected wild plant. Wild populations: Extremely rare; fewer than 11 natural populations. Despite EN status, species is secure through extensive cultivation worldwide.

Sacred in Buddhism, Taoism, Confucianism, Shinto. Buddhist monks preserved species through temple plantings. Symbol of longevity, hope, resilience, peace. Hiroshima: Six trees survived 1945 atomic bomb. Japan: On 100+ family crests; Tokyo symbol. Medicine: 2000+ years in TCM.
Deciduous. One of few deciduous gymnosperms. Leaves turn brilliant golden-yellow in autumn, then drop rapidly, often within a single night. Autumn leaf drop is notably synchronous and dramatic.

Generally pest/disease free. Occasional: Aphids (minor), scale (rare). Diseases: Phytophthora root rot (avoid waterlogging), Armillaria (rare). Natural resistance from leaf fungicides. Maintain vigor and drainage.

Limited ecological function in wild due to rarity. Wildlife: Seeds eaten by some mammals. Pollination: Wind-pollinated. Urban ecology: Important urban tree providing shade and pollution absorption. Cultural ecology: Sacred groves at Buddhist temples have preserved genetic diversity.
Natural wild populations: 300-1250 meters. Mt. Tianmu (Zhejiang): 300-1250m. Dalou Mountains (Guizhou): 840-1200m. Cultivation: Primarily lowlands but adaptable to wide range.

Genus name Ginkgo is a misrendering of Japanese gin (silver) + kyo (apricot), referring to silver-colored seeds; the misspelling originated with Engelbert Kaempfer in 1712 and was perpetuated by Linnaeus. Species name biloba from Latin bis (twice) + loba (lobed), referring to the bilobed leaf shape.
Fire resistance: Moderate to good. Recovery: Sprouts from base after top-kill. Can regenerate from embedded buds. No special management needed; natural resilience adequate.

Gymnosperm - no true flowers. Male: Catkin-like pollen cones, yellowish, 2-3cm. Female: Paired ovules on stalks, greenish. Pollination: Wind-pollinated in spring. Dioecious. Sex may take 20+ years to determine.

Seeds with fleshy outer layer (not true fruit). Size: 2-3cm. Shape: Plum-like. Color: Yellowish. Seed coat: Fleshy sarcotesta (foul-smelling), hard sclerotesta, papery endotesta. Inner kernel: Edible ginkgo nut. Odor: Strong unpleasant smell. Maturation: Autumn.

Ginkgo biloba is a large, long-lived deciduous gymnosperm tree native to southeastern China, the sole surviving species of the ancient division Ginkgophyta. Known as a living fossil, the species has remained virtually unchanged for over 200 million years. It grows 20-35m tall with distinctive fan-shaped, bilobed leaves that turn golden-yellow in autumn.

Large deciduous tree. Shape: Pyramidal when young; irregular with age. Single trunk, sparse branching with distinctive short shoots (spurs). Capable of producing aerial chichi (prop roots). Dioecious: separate male and female trees.

Natural habitat: Disturbed streamside environments in deciduous forests on acidic loess soils with good drainage. Wild populations restricted to mountainous areas of southeastern China (Mt. Tianmu, Dalou Mountains). Elevations: 300-1250m. Shows preference for disturbed sites. Cultivation: Extremely adaptable; thrives in urban environments worldwide.

Unique fan-shaped leaves with dichotomous (forking) venation, usually bilobed. Deciduous gymnosperm. Leaves 5-10cm long, bright green turning golden-yellow in autumn. Dioecious: male trees produce catkin-like pollen cones; female trees produce foul-smelling fleshy seeds. Bark gray, deeply furrowed on older trees. Pyramidal shape when young.

Simple, alternate, deciduous. Shape: Fan-shaped with notched margin; often deeply cleft creating two lobes. Size: 5-10cm. Venation: Unique dichotomous pattern. Color: Bright green; golden-yellow in autumn. Clustered on short shoots.
Typical: 1,000+ years. Maximum confirmed: 1,600+ years. Claims of 3,500 years unsubstantiated. Research shows no programmed senescence; death from external factors only. One of longest-lived trees.
Maximum trunk diameter: Up to 2.5m (8 ft) DBH. Typical mature: 1-2m. Some ancient specimens exceed 10m girth.
Typical: 20-35m (65-115 ft). Maximum: Up to 50m (164 ft). Cultivated: 15-25m common. Growth rate: 30-60cm/year when young. Crown spread: 9-15m at maturity.

Oldest reliable: ~1,600 years. Claims to 3,500 years unverified. Famous specimens: Gu Guanyin Temple (~1,400 yrs); numerous 1,000+ year trees at temples. Six Hiroshima survivor trees (1945) still thrive.

Native to: Southeastern China only (Zhejiang, Guizhou). Glacial refugia: Southwestern China, Eastern China, Southern China. Introduced: China, Japan, Korea, Europe, North America. Climate: Temperate to Mediterranean; mean annual temp -3.3 to 23.3C; precipitation 34-3925mm.

Leaves: Source of medicinal extract (EGb 761); major commercial product. Seeds: Edible ginkgo nuts (cooked only). Leaf extract: Herbal supplement industry (billions annually). Ornamental: Fall foliage tourism. Traditional medicine: Seeds and leaves in TCM. Bonsai: Popular subject.

Ginkgo nuts: Low protein (5%), low fat (1%), rich in carbohydrates. Vitamins: B-complex, C. Minerals: Potassium, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, iron, zinc. CAUTION: Contains ginkgotoxin; max 10 cooked nuts/day adults, 6/day children. Raw nuts toxic. Outer flesh causes dermatitis.

Seed: Remove flesh (wear gloves); warm stratify 6-8 weeks at 20-30C; cold stratify 6-8 weeks at 5C; germination 30-60 days. Cuttings: Summer softwood, 8000ppm IBA, 6-8 weeks rooting. Grafting: Most common commercial method for cultivars.

Maidenhair Tree (English, most common); Ginkgo (English, from Japanese); Gingko (alternate spelling); Icho (Japanese); Yinxing, Baiguo (Chinese, meaning silver apricot, white fruit); Eunhaeng (Korean); Duck Foot Tree (from leaf shape)

Seed: Fresh seeds germinate after stratification; sex unknown until maturity. Cuttings: Softwood with hormone; slow. Grafting: Most common commercial; ensures cultivar/sex. Layering: Air layering possible.
Timing: Late winter/early spring. Young: Train central leader. Mature: Minimal needed. Never top. Wound response: Slow; avoid large cuts. Tolerates pruning but rarely requires it.

Site: Full sun; well-drained soil. Planting: Spring or fall; water 3-5 years. Sex: Plant male cultivars to avoid seeds. Spacing: 9-15m. Water: Drought-tolerant once established. Fertilization: Rarely needed. Pruning: Minimal; late winter.

Salisburia adiantifolia Sm.; Salisburia biloba (L.) Hoffmanns.; Pterophyllus salisburiensis J.Nelson. The species has remarkably few synonyms given its long taxonomic history, as it is the sole surviving member of its entire division.

claim_value: Type: Softwood (gymnosperm). Color: Pale yellow to light orange-brown. Soft, light, fine texture. Uses: Carvings, cutting boards, sushi boards, game boards, sake containers, religious objects. Not structural. Availability: Limited; urban tree removals.

Pollution: Exceptional tolerance. Drought: Good once established. Salt: Moderate. Pests: Highly resistant. Diseases: Highly resistant. Deer: Highly resistant. Compaction: Tolerates urban soils. Wind: Moderate tolerance.
